name: Amarone della Valpolicella

climate.koppen_name: Temperate, no dry season, hot summer

climate: Seasons this warm ripen Merlot, Sémillon, Cabernet Franc, Tempranillo and Dolcetto fully without cooking off their freshness.
Merlot sits in its sweet spot, so the wines can show the style it is known for.
Pinot Gris is at its warm limit. It can ripen too fast, giving heavy, soft wine that has lost its freshness.

soil.rock: Limestone makes alkaline soil that drains well yet can hold water for the vines. It is usually planted to grapes valued for their acidity.
soil.top: The topsoil holds water well and drains at a steady pace, so vines rarely go thirsty or sit in wet ground. Its pH is close to neutral, so vines take up the nutrients they need easily.

land: The high ground runs about 7°F cooler than the low ground. Higher vineyards ripen later and keep more acidity, so one grape can make lighter or richer wine here depending on height.
Much of it is steep. Cold air and rain run off, so frost and waterlogging are rare and soils stay thin, keeping yields low. Steep rows are slow and costly to work, often by hand.

winkler: Good for generous crops of standard to good wine.

sheet.place: Amarone is a dry, full red from Verona. Corvina, Corvinone and Rondinella grapes are dried for months, then pressed no earlier than December. It needs at least 14% alcohol and two years of aging.

claims.claim: The DOCG covers Amarone della Valpolicella, which may add Classico or Valpantena, and the word Riserva.

Corvina and/or Corvinone must be 45% to 95% of the vineyard. Rondinella must be 5% to 30%. Up to 25% in total may be other authorised red grapes: at most 15% non-aromatic reds from the Verona list (no single grape over 10%), and the rest native Italian reds.

The wider zone is all or part of 19 communes in the province of Verona, including Negrar, Marano, Fumane, Sant'Ambrogio, San Pietro in Cariano, Dolcè, Verona itself, Grezzana, Illasi and Tregnago. Vineyards on peaty or very wet valley-floor soil are excluded.

The Classico zone is the communes of Negrar, Marano, Fumane, Sant'Ambrogio and San Pietro in Cariano. Valpantena is a separately delimited valley zone to the north of Verona, bounded in part by the 500 m contour.

Grapes are dried (appassimento) in suitable rooms before pressing. Climate-controlled rooms are allowed if they run at temperatures like traditional drying. Heat-assisted dehumidifying is banned. Drying is not given a fixed time or weight loss.
Dried grapes cannot be vinified before 1 December, unless the Veneto Region allows it earlier after a documented request from the Consorzio. The dried grapes must reach at least 14% natural alcohol.
The official description of the wine says the grapes are held in drying lofts (fruttai) for about 100 to 120 days. This is a description, not a legal minimum.
Wine from dried grapes may not exceed 40% of the grape weight. The Region can lower this each year at the Consorzio's request.
Producers say the grapes lose roughly 40% to 50% of their weight while drying, over about three to four months.
Amarone must age at least two years, counted from 1 January after the harvest, before sale. Riserva needs at least four years from 1 November of the harvest year.

The descriptive section of the disciplinare says the wine spends at least two years in wooden containers, then is bottled and rests more in bottle before release. The operative aging article does not name wood or barrel size.

Finished wine must have at least 14% actual alcohol, at least 5.0 g/l total acidity and 28 g/l extract (32 g/l for Riserva). Residual sugar is capped at 9 g/l at 14%, with a small allowance for each extra 0.1% alcohol.

The disciplinare describes a deep red that can turn garnet with age, with a strong nose of raisined fruit, tobacco and spice. The palate is full, velvety and warm. It calls Amarone one of the longest-lived great Italian wines.

Amarone was first recognised as a type of Valpolicella by DPR of 21 August 1968. The disciplinare says four wines (Valpolicella, Ripasso, Recioto, Amarone) were made autonomous denominations by ministerial decrees of 24 March 2010.
Amarone and Recioto della Valpolicella were promoted to DOCG on 4 December 2009. English Wikipedia also gives DOC status as 1990.

The disciplinare says the first commercial bottle of Amarone della Valpolicella dates from 1953. It traces the style's ancestor to Acinatico, a dried-grape wine asked for by Cassiodorus in the 4th to 6th century letters.
Valpolicella soils come from broken-down limestone and dolomite rock, from basalt, and from glacial and river deposits of volcanic origin. They vary, so water supply to the vines varies too.
Bertani describes Valpantena as a pre-alpine valley with ferruginous marl and clay-limestone marl soils. Albino Armani describes Classico high-hill sites as calcareous deposits on volcanic rock.
Vineyards reach up to about 500 m above sea level.

On low and middle hills and valley floors vines mostly face south. Higher up, vineyards sit on the gentler ridge tops and near-flat tops of the higher hills, on both the west and east sides of the zone.
Vines must be trained on a trellis (spalliera) or an inclined Veronese pergola. Vines must be at least in their fourth growing cycle to count.
The climate is mild and not very rainy, sheltered by the Lessini mountains to the north and near Lake Garda. Yearly rain is about 850 to 1,000 mm, mostly in winter.
Amarone is Italian for 'great bitter', from amaro with the -one augmentative. It set the dry wine apart from the sweet Recioto made in the same place.
A popular story says a forgotten cask of Recioto fermented dry and Adelino Lucchese of the Valpolicella cooperative called it 'Amarone' in 1936.
